newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's Chubais defends record before budget vote.
newsitem.headline: Russia's Chubais defends record before budget vote.

text.p: First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais defended his government's economic record on Tuesday ahead of a crucial parliamentary vote on spending cuts needed to bring order to the country's chaotic finances.

Chubais, the reshuffled government's chief reformer, said sound finances were the bedrock of a market economy and urged his communist opponents in the State Duma lower house of parliament to approve the spending plans and a new tax code.
"We consider that order in the state must start with finances, and especially with the state's own finances," Chubais told members of the upper house Federation Council.

Chubais, in charge of the government while Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin is on vacation, said the government had to cut spending across the board to offset poor tax collection and ensure that 1997 budget deficit targets were met.

He said tough parameters for the 1998 budget had already been fixed and would include the scrapping of tax breaks and subsidies. "They will be real figures and we will be answerable to you for them," said Chubais, who is also finance minister.
The draft 1998 budget is based on a government-proposed tax code. Chubais urged deputies to approve the first reading of the new tax code before the summer recess starts on June 21.
The code aims to make Russia's convoluted tax system more workable and transparent.

The Duma, dominated by the opposition, is very angry about the proposed spending cuts but on Tuesday Communist Party chief Gennady Zyuganov sounded a conciliatory note, suggesting that a special commission could be set up to examine the plans.
"Every point of the sequestration plan has to be analysed professionally," Interfax news agency quoted Zyuganov as saying.

The Duma, which wants to avoid a head-on collision with the government, is also expected on Wednesday to consider a resolution condemning Russia's privatisation campaign in 1992-1996, spearheaded by Chubais.
A proposal to be considered by the Duma on Wednesday would leave the cabinet free to cut spending but also to take full responsibility for the social consequences.

Chubais said a series of extraordinary measures would bring some 34 trillion roubles of additional budget revenues, mostly from Russia's major tax debtors such as Gazprom gas monopoly, carmaker AvtoVaz and Sibneft and Nizhnevartovskneftegaz oil firms.
He said the government also aimed to lower tariffs for so-called natural monopolies -- gas, electricity and transport -- and to slash costly housing subsidies to help ease pressure on local budgets.
Chubais, a hate figure for the opposition, said the state had an important but limited role to play in a market economy.
"We are for strengthening the role of the state, for re-establishing it where it was lost, but we have to act wisely to reach this target," Chubais told the Federation Council.
Chubais has been invited to address the Duma on Wednesday but if he goes he is unlikely to receive a very cordial welcome.
On Tuesday the Duma's communist speaker Gennady Seleznyov accused Chubais of ignoring Russia's own unique historical conditions in his drive to establish Western-style capitalism.

The announcement on Tuesday that Chubais earned seven times as much as President Boris Yeltsin in 1996 will do nothing to improve the unpopular minister's image in a country where the average monthly pay is arund $145.
Reports about Chubais's wealth have outraged opposition deputies, though Russian media say the authorities have found no evidence that he acquired his wealth unfairly.
His personal income has been boosted by lecture fees and profits on securities trade, Interfax news agency said.
